stem_md:
In the triangle \(ABC\), let \(I\) be the incenter. Denote \(X\) as the intersection of \(BC\) and the perpendicular bisector of \(AI\), \(Y\) as the intersection of \(CA\) and the perpendicular bisector of \(BI\), and \(Z\) as the intersection of \(AB\) and the perpendicular bisector of \(CI\). 

Prove that the circumcircles of \(\triangle AIX\), \(\triangle BIY\), and \(\triangle CIZ\) are coaxial. 

*Proposed by Yuan Zhang, Shijiazhuang No. 2 High School*

**Attachments:**

![graph.png](https://cdn.artofproblemsolving.com/attachments/b/8/905bf4f3e507bb6a4cd46d57db6e3b7b7edc8f.png)
solution_md:
No entiendo complejos entonces vamos a generalizar y resolver el problema que dijo dotted.
Sea $ABC$ un triángulo, $P$ un punto en su neuberg cubic. Definimos $O_a$ , $O_b$ y $O_c$ como los centros de $(BPC)$ , $(CPA)$ y $(APB)$ respectiamente, los triángulos $ABC$ y $O_aO_bO_c$ son perspectivos en $Q$ . Demuestra que las reflexiones de $AP$ , $BP$ y $CP$ por $AQ$ , $BQ$ y $CQ$ respectiamente concurren.
Sea $P*$ el conjugado isogonal de $P$ . Vamos a mover $P$ en la neuberg cubic con grado 3. Veamos que la recta $BP$ y $CP$ tienen grado 2 por zack's lemma (ya no podemos usar $B$ y $C$ en los casos finales), ahora $BP*$ y $CP*$ tienen grado 2, entonces $P*$ tiene grado 3 por zack's lemma con $P=A$ . Es hecho conocido de la neuberg cubic que $Q=X(3)P\cap X(4)P*$ entonces $Q$ tiene grado 3 por zack's lemma con $P=X(3), X(4), X(30)$ . Notemos que $AP$ tiene grado 2 por zack's con $P=A$ entonces $\infty_{AP}$ y $\infty_{\perp AP}$ tienen grado 2, la recta $AQ$ también tiene grado 2 por zack's lemma tomando $P=AX(3) \cap (BX(3)C)$ . Ahora $P_a=AQ \cap P\infty_{\perp AP}$ tiene grado 2+3+2=7. Podemos reflejar $P$ por $P_a$ con Roge-Ransom lemma, entonces ese punto $T_a$ tiene grado 3+7-k donde $P$ y $P_a$ son ambos puntos al infinito en $k$ casos pero tomando $P=X(30)$ y $P$ como los circle points tenemos que ambos son puntos al infinito, entonces $T_a$ tiene grado 7. Basta demostrar 22 casos para ver que $AT_a$ , $BT_b$ y $CT_c$ concurren, además es simple ver que si $P$ es un caso que funciona entonces $P*$ también funciona ya que $Q$ se cambia por su isogonal.
Cuatro casosConsidera $P$ como el incentro y los tres excentros, la concurrencia se cumple por conjugados isogonales.
Tres casosConsidera $P$ como la reflexión de $A$ por $BC$ , es fácil ver que $Q$ queda en $BC$ y el punto de concurrencia es $A$ . Toma de manera cíclica las reflexiones de $B$ y $C$ .
Seis casosToma $P$ tal que $BPC$ es un triángulo equilatero, puedes ver que $Q$ es el centro de $BPC$ y el punto de concurrencia esta en $BC$ . $P$ puede estar de cada lado respecto a $BC$ y los casos cíclicos.
Seis casosTe tomas el conjugado isogonal de los seis casos anteriores.
Dos casosConsidera $P=X(13)$ . Este es más complicado pero puedes demostrarlo fijando $B$ , $C$ , $X(13)$ y la recta $AX(13)$ , luego varias $A$ en $AX(13)$ y calculas los grados con algún zack's lemma, los casos útiles eran $A$ tal que $ABC$ fuer isosceles (da cuatro casos), $A$ tal que $X(13)$ fuera el incentro o el excentro de $ABC$ y $A$ como el centro $BX(13)C$ . De manera análoga puedes ver que $P=X(14)$ funciona.
Dos casosTe tomas el conjugado isogonal de los dos casos anteriores.
Creo que en realidad basta hacer 19 casos porque al tomar $P=A$ te queda $A=P=P_a=T_a$ y $AT_a$ tendría grado 6 por zack's lemma pero no estaba seguro porque ya usamos ese caso en un zack's anterior.

Inverting at  $I$  and rewriting the reference frame gives the following problem:

In triangle  $ABC$ ,  $A'$  is the reflection of  $O$  over  $BC$ . Show that the reflection of  $AH$  over  $AA'$  and other cyclic permutations concur.

In complex, the line  $AH$  has equation  $z-bc\overline z=a-\frac{bc}a$ , and line  $AA'$  has equation  $z-\frac{abc(b+c-a)}{ab+ac-bc}\overline z=a-\frac{bc(b+c-a)}{ab+ac-bc}$ , so the reflection has equation

\begin{align*}
z-\frac{a^2bc(b+c-a)^2}{(ab+ac-bc)^2}\overline z&=a-\frac{abc(b+c-a)^2}{(ab+ac-bc)^2}
(ab+ac-bc)^2z-a^2bc(b+c-a)^2\overline z&=a(ab+ac-bc)^2-abc(b+c-a)^2
(ab+ac-bc)^2z-a^2bc(b+c-a)^2\overline z&=a(a^2b^2+a^2c^2+b^2c^2+bc(a^2-(b+c)^2))
(ab+ac-bc)^2z-a^2bc(b+c-a)^2\overline z&=a(a^2-bc)(b^2+c^2+bc)
\end{align*}

Multiply this equation by  $b-c$  and take the cyclic sum. We claim the result is  $0$ , which solves the problem. We have
\begin{align*}
(b-c)(ab+ac-bc)^2&=(b-c)(ab+ac+bc)^2-4abc(b-c)(b+c)
(b-c)a^2bc(b+c-a)^2&=abc(a+b+c)^2a(b-c)-4abca^2(b^2-c^2)
(b-c)a(a^2-bc)(b^2+c^2+bc)&=a(b-c)(b+c)^2(a^2-bc)-abc(b-c)(a^2-bc)
&=(b^2-c^2)a^3(b+c)-abc(b-c)(a+b)(a+c)
&=(b^2-c^2)a^3(b+c)-abc(a+b+c)a(b-c)-ab^2c^2(b-c)
&=-abc(a+b+c)a(b-c)+a(b-c)(a^2(b+c)^2-b^2c^2)
&=-abc(a+b+c)a(b-c)+a(b-c)(a^2b^2+a^2c^2+b^2c^2)-2abc(b-c)(a^2-bc).
\end{align*}

All of these have cyclic sum equal to  $0$ , so they concur.

stem_md:
For positive integers \( n \) and positive real numbers \( a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n \), define  
\[[a_1, a_2, \cdots, a_n] = \frac{1}{a_1 + \frac{1}{a_2 + \frac{1}{\cdots + \frac{1}{a_n}}}}. \]  
Determine the minimal real number \( C \) such that for any positive real numbers \( x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_{2024} \),
\[[x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_{2024}] - [x_1^2, x_2^2, \cdots, x_{2024}^2] \leq C. \]  
*Proposed by Ruixuan Zhu*
solution_md:
Very nice problem! The proposer is also just one step away from this year's CHN team :blush: 
------
The answer is  $253.$  **Construction:**  $x_1=x_3=\cdots =x_{2023}=\varepsilon$  and  $x_2=x_4=\cdots =x_{2024}=1/2$  where  $\varepsilon\to 0^+.$ **Proof.** We induct on  $n$  to prove that  $[x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_{2n}] - [x_1^2, x_2^2, \cdots, x_{2n}^2] \leq n/4.$   $n=1$  is easy to prove.
Assume  $n$  holds, consider  $n+1,$  since by induction hypothesis,
\[[x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_{2n+2}]=\dfrac{1}{x_1+\dfrac {1}{x_2+[x_3, \cdots, x_{2n+2}]}}\le  \dfrac{1}{x_1+\dfrac {1}{x_2^2+1/4+[x_3^2, \cdots, x_{2n+2}^2]}},\]
we are left only trivial calculations(lazy to write). $\Box$ ------
The idea of official solution is to prove
\[\frac 1n[x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_{2n}] ^2\le[x_1^2, x_2^2, \cdots, x_{2n}^2]\]
by induction, which leaves less calculation.

The author also gives some generalizations on an article in NSmath, I studied a lot from it :-D  (left as attachment).

**Attachments:**

[Inequalities_compressed.pdf](https://cdn.artofproblemsolving.com/attachments/2/a/7aed1dbaa4a8a379688b9afaa4a3b65bafeacd.pdf)

stem_md:
Given positive integers \( m, n \), determine the smallest positive integer \( k \) with the following property:

For any \( 2k \) integers \( a_1, a_2, \cdots, a_k, b_1, b_2, \cdots, b_k \), there always exist two non-empty subsets \( I, J \subseteq \{1, 2, \cdots, k\} \) satisfying   $$ |I| = |J| ;\quad m\, \bigg|\sum_{i \in I} a_i ;\quad n\, \bigg|\sum_{j \in J} b_j. $$  *Proposed by Tianqin Li*
solution_md:
Qute problem generalizing the EGZ Thm.  :-D 
------
The answer is  $(m,n)+[m,n]-1.$  When  $k=(m,n)+[m,n]-2,$  all  $a_i=1,$  and  $b_1=\cdots =b_{(m,n)-1}=0,b_{(m,n)}=\cdots =b_k=1$  is a counterexample(easy to verify).

Let  $(m,n)=d$ ,  $m=dm_1,$   $n=dn_1,$  we show that  $k=d(m_1n_1+1)-1$  satisfies the condition.
By EGZ Thm, we may find  $d$  numbers with sum multiple of  $d$  in every  $2d-1$  numbers, therefore there exists  $dm_1n_1$  numbers in  $a_i,$  and a partition of  $m_1n_1$  groups(with  $d$  numbers each group), in each group the sum is a multiple of  $d$ . Call them  $dX_1,\cdots ,dX_{m_1n_1}.$  We can also find  $dY_1,\cdots ,dY_{m_1n_1}$  in  $b_i$ s by this way.

Now note that in every  $m_1$  numbers there are some of them, with sum multiple of  $m_1,$  therefore we may find  $S_1,\cdots ,S_u$  such that  $|S_i|\le m_1$  and  $|[m_1n_1]\backslash (S_1\cup\cdots \cup S_u)|<m_1,$   $u\ge n_1,$  and in each  $S_i,$  those sum are multiple of  $m_1.$  Now since there is a sum of muptiple of  $n_1$  in every  $n_1$  numbers. We get our desired result. $\Box$

stem_md:
Let \( n \) be a positive integer. An "\( n \)-calculator" has a display screen and four buttons. The display screen shows a real number. Suppose the number currently displayed is \( x \). The four buttons can replace the number \( x \) on the display with  
\[x + n, \quad x - n, \quad \frac{x}{nx + 1}, \quad \frac{x}{-nx + 1}.\]
Specifically, if \( x = -\frac{1}{n} \), the third button cannot be pressed; if \( x = \frac{1}{n} \), the fourth button cannot be pressed.

A rational number \( q \) is said to be *reachable* if there exists a rational number \( p = \frac{s}{t} \) (where \( s \) and \( t \) are integers with absolute values not exceeding  $2024$ , and \( t \neq 0 \)), such that if the "\( n \)-calculator" initially displays \( p \), then through a finite number (possibly zero) of appropriate button presses, the number displayed on the calculator can become \( q \).

(1) Find all positive integers \( n \) such that every rational number is reachable;  

(2) Find all positive integers \( n \) such that there exists a positive constant \( C \) satisfying: for any positive integer \( m \), the number of reachable rational numbers of the form \( \frac{a}{b} \) (where \( a \) and \( b \) are integers with absolute values not exceeding \( m \), and \( b \neq 0 \)) is at most \( Cm^{1.99} \).  

*Proposed by Hanqing Huang and Cheng Jiang*
solution_md:
Replace the operations with  $\frac1x$  and  $x\pm n$ . This is equivalent to the original problem.

(1)  $n=1$  and  $n=2$  work by the Euclidean algorithm. If  $n\geq 3$ , consider the reverse, where we try to reduce a number to a number with small numerator and denominator. Cancel all consecutive applications of  $\frac1x$  and opposite signs of  $\pm n$ . Define  $f(\frac ab)=|a|+|b|$ . The reciprocal operation preserves  $f$ , while  $\pm n$  increases  $f$  for all  $|x|\leq 1$ . If reciprocal is ever applied to a number with absolute value greater than  $1$ , then  $f$  never decreases and must keep increasing, contradiction. Therefore, the reciprocal operation must only be done when  $|x|\leq 1$ . However,  $x=\frac{10001}{10000}$  is a contradiction.

stem_md:
Let real numbers \( x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_{100} \) satisfy that  
\[|x_1 - x_2|, |x_2 - x_3|, \cdots, |x_{99} - x_{100}|, |x_{100} - x_1|\]  
is a permutation of \( 1, 2, \cdots, 100 \). Let \( M \) and \( m \) be the maximum and minimum of \( x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_{100} \), respectively. Find all possible values of \( M - m \).
solution_md:
The maximum  $M-m$  is  $2525$ , achievable by partitioning  $[100]$  into two groups with sum  $2525$  and letting the numbers range from  $0$  to  $2525$  with the positive differences consecutively in one group and the negative differences consecutively in the other group. For any range less than  $2525$ , let the range be  $r$  where  $r\geq100$ . Greedily pick some numbers which add to  $2525-r$ . The remaining numbers will be between  $1$  and  $x$  excluding at most one number in this range. The sum of the numbers is  $2525+r$ , which is at least  $2600$ , and every number between  $1$  and this sum is achievable unless  $1$  or  $2$  is removed, which implies all numbers except the number removed and the total minus the number removed are possible as sums. In particular,  $2525$  is a possible sum, so we have three sets of numbers with sum  $r$ ,  $2525-r$ , and  $2525$ . If  $r\geq199$ , then first go from  $0$  to  $r$  using the differences in the set with sum  $r$ . Then, use the set with sum  $2525-r$  as a positive difference and the set with sum  $2525$  as a negative difference to get back to  $0$ , which is always possible when  $r\geq199$ .

If  $100\leq r\leq 199$ , then first go  $0$ ,  $100$ ,  $1$ ,  $99$ , ...,  $30$ ,  $70$ . The differences less than  $40$  still remain. By the same argument, we can get three sets with sums  $r-70$ ,  $425$ , and  $425-r$ , so we can use the same construction from before.

Clearly,  $r<100$  and  $r>2525$  is impossible.

solution_md: **Solution 94:** Let $\omega = \odot(S,SB)$ ; $\Omega = \odot(ABC)$ ; $O$ be center of $\omega$ ; $T$ be antipode of $S$ wrt $\omega$ ; $M$ be the midpoint of segment $PQ$ . Note $PQ$ passes through $O$ .**Claim 1: ** $P,Q$ are isogonal conjugates wrt $\triangle ABC$ . *Proof:* This is because $AP,AQ$ are isogonal wrt $\angle A$ and $\angle BPC + \angle BQC = 180^\circ + \angle A$ . In other words, if $P^*$ is the isogonal conjugate of $P$ wrt $\triangle ABC$ , then $P^* \in AQ$ and $\angle BQC = \angle BPC$ . Hence $P^* \equiv Q$ . An alternate way to see this is: If $I$ is incenter of $\triangle ABC$ , then $IP = IQ$ , so then subtend equal angles on $\omega$ , which implies our Claim. $\square$ **Claim 2: ** $SA_1 = SA_2 = B_1B_2 = C_1C_2$ . *Proof:* Observe that $$ \angle PBQ = \angle PCQ = \frac{\angle PSQ}{2} ~ \textcolor{blue}{\textbf{=}} ~ \frac{\angle PAQ}{2} = \angle SAP = \angle SAQ $$ So arcs $\widehat{SA_1},\widehat{SA_2},\widehat{B_1B_2},\widehat{C_1C_2}$ subtend equal angles on circumference of $\Omega$ , and hence they are equal in length. $\square$ **Claim 3: ** perpendicular bisector of segments $AT,M_2M_3$ coincides, particularly points $A,T,M_2,M_3$ are concyclic. *Proof:* Let $S_2,S_3$ be midpoint of arcs $\widehat{AC},\widehat{AB}$ of $\Omega$ not containing $C,A$ , respectively. Note $O-M_2-S_2$ and $O-M_3-S_3$ . Further, as $B_1B_2 = C_1C_2$ , so $OM_2 = OM_3$ . It follows segments $M_2M_3,S_2S_3$ have same perpendicular bisector. On the other hand, it is well known that segments $S_2S_3,AT$ have same perpendicular bisector. This proves our Claim. $\square$ **(Key) Claim 4: ** $M_3$ is circumcenter of $\triangle AMB$ . Similarly $M_2$ is circumenter of $\triangle AMC$ . *Proof:* Note $B$ is the center of spiral similarity $\sigma$ sending $C_2 \to Q$ and $C_1 \to P$ . Note, $$ \sigma ~:~ M_3 \to M ~~,~~ O \to S $$ So we obtain $$ \triangle BM_3O \sim \triangle BMS \implies \triangle BM_3M \sim \triangle BOS $$ Since $OB = OS$ , thus $M_3B = M_3M$ . Also, $M_3B = M_3A$ . So our Claim is proven. $\square$ It follows that $M_2M_3$ is perpendicular bisector of segment $AM$ . Let $X$ be midpoint of segment $OT$ . It follows (by looking at $S$ ) that $$ \boxed{X \in M_2M_3} $$ Because of **Claim 3**, we just have to show that points $M_1,M_2,M_3,T$ are concylic. Let $\Gamma$ be the circle with center $O$ passing through midpoint of segments $SA_1,SA_2$ . Due to **Claim 2** we obtain $$ M_2,M_3 \in \Gamma $$ Hence it suffices to show $$ \text{Pow}_{\Gamma}(X) = XT \cdot XM_1 $$ Let $Y$ be midpoint of segment $SA_1$ . Observe that \begin{align*} XT \cdot XM_1 &= \frac{XM_1 \cdot XS}{3} = \frac{SX^2 - SM_1 \cdot SX}{3} = \frac{SX^2}{3} - \frac{SM_1 \cdot ST}{4} = \frac{SX^2}{3} - \frac{SA_1^2}{4} = 3OX^2 - SY^2 \text{Pow}_{\Gamma}(X) &= OY^2 - OX^2 = OS^2 - SY^2 - OX^2 = (2OX)^2 - OX^2 - SY^2 = 3OX^2 - SY^2 \end{align*} This completes the proof. $\blacksquare$ **Remark: ** I can't find a synthetic proof for showing $$ \text{Pow}_{\Gamma}(X) = XT \cdot XM_1 $$ One gets that homothety $\mathbb H$ at $S$ at scale factor $2$ sends $\Gamma$ to $\odot(T,TA_1)$ . The point $Z := \mathbb H(X) = 2X - S = 2T-O$ is also nice. But I can't get much progress from this.

Trivial by the following two lemma:(*Please get some of the knowledges of Orthotransversals and some conics first* :D) We denote the **orthotransversal** of $X$ w.r.t. $\triangle ABC$ be $\mathcal{O}_{X}(\triangle ABC)$ . Now given a triangle $ABC$ . As usual, we have $H$ be the orthocenter. $\boxed{\textbf{Lemma 1.}}$
$\mathcal{O}_{X}(\triangle ABC)$ is perpendicular of tangent of $X$ w.r.t the conic passing through $A,B,C,H,X$
$\boxed{\textbf{Lemma 2.}}$
$\mathcal{O}_{X}(\triangle ABC)$ , the trillinear polar of $X$ w.r.t. $\triangle ABC$ , the polar of $X$ w.r.t. the pedal circle of $P$ are concurrent.
$\boxed{\textbf{Back to the main problem}}$ Consider conic $ABCHI_a$ , by $\textbf{Lemma 1.}$ we have $\mathcal{O}_{I_a}(\triangle ABC)\perp I_aI_{a(ABCHI_a)}$ . By $\textbf{Lemma 2.}$ we have $\mathcal{O}_{I_a}(\triangle ABC),EF,\mathcal L_{\infty}$ are concurrent. But it's well-known that conic $ABCHI_a$ is the isogonal conjugate of $OI_a$ and $I_a$ fixes under the isogonal transformation, hence $I_aI_{a(ABCHI_a)}\equiv OI_a$ , as desired. $\quad\blacksquare$

Redefine  $X = \overline{PQ} \cap \overline{EF}$ . We will show that  $A$ ,  $X$ ,  $S$  are collinear.

First, we use barycentrics wrt  $AEF$ . Swap the labels of  $B$  and  $E$ ,  $C$  and  $F$ , and replace  $H$  with  $A'$ . From a certain [url = https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c792843h2620365_more_geo_because_im_bored]helpful handout[/url], we know that  $A' = (-S_{BC}:b^2S_B:c^2S_C)$ , so  $E = (-S_B:0:c^2) = (-\tfrac{S_B}{S_A},0,\tfrac{c^2}{S_A})$ . It follows that  $Q = 2C-E = (S_B:0:b^2-a^2)$ . By symmetry  $P = (S_C:c^2-a^2:0)$ , so if  $X = (0,t,1-t)$ ,   $$ 0 = \begin{vmatrix}0 & t & 1-t  S_B & 0 & b^2-a^2  S_C & c^2-a^2 & 0\end{vmatrix}. $$   Solving gives  $X = (0:S_B(a^2-c^2):S_C(a^2-b^2))$ .

Now we switch the reference triangle back to  $ABC$ , and switch back the labels as well. Since  $\overline{EF}$  is antiparallel to  $\overline{BC}$ , by isogonality, we have  $X' := \overline{AX} \cap \overline{BC} = (0:\tfrac{b^2}{S_B(a^2-c^2)}:\tfrac{c^2}{S_C(a^2-b^2)})$ . Also if  $K = \overline{LH} \cap \overline{BC} = (0,t,1-t)$ , we have   $$ 0 = \begin{vmatrix}0 & t & 1-t  S_{BC} & S_{CA} & S_{AB}  a^2 & b^2 & c^2 \end{vmatrix} $$   from where we get  $K = (0:S_C(b^2S_B-a^2S_A):S_B(c^2S_C-a^2S_A))$ . 

Let  $D = \overline{AH} \cap \overline{BC}$  and  $H_A = \overline{AH} \cap (ABC) \setminus A$ . By definition  $K-S-H_A$ , so if  $S' = \overline{AX} \cap (ABC) \setminus A$ , it suffices to show that  $K-S'-H_A$ . 

By Ratio lemma, if  $f(V) = \frac{VC}{VB}$ , then the result is equivalent to   $$ f(K) = f(S')f(H_A) = \frac{f(X')}{f(A)} \frac{f(D)}{f(A)} = \frac{c^2}{b^2} f(X')f(D). $$   We know that  $f(K) = \frac{S_C(b^2S_B-a^2S_A)}{S_B(c^2S_C-a^2S_A)}$ , and since  $D = (0:S_C:S_B)$ , we have   $$ f(S')f(H_A) = \frac{c^2}{b^2} \frac{b^2/(S_B(a^2-c^2))}{c^2/(S_C(a^2-b^2))}\frac{S_C}{S_B} = \frac{S_C^2(a^2-b^2)}{S_B^2(a^2-c^2)}. $$   But by expansion  $S_C(a^2-b^2) = b^2S_B - a^2S_A$ , so we are done.</details>

Lemma: In triangle  $ABC, O$  is the circumcenter,  $O_A$  is the circumcenter of  $OBC$ .  $M,N$  are the projections of  $O_A$  on  $AB,AC$ . Let I be the circumcenter of  $AMN$  and  $I_A$  be the circumcenter of  $IBC$ . Then   $$ \angle (O_AI_A;AB,AC)= 90-C, 90-B $$  Actually by homothety this true for any point on  $AO_A$ , in particular for Kosnita Point.

Proof: Let  $N_9$  be the nine-point center. Let  $F$  be the midpoint of  $XY$  where  $X,Y$  are the intersections of  $(OBC)$  with  $AC,AB$ .  $E$  is the midpoint of  $BC$ .

Claim:  $N_9-F-I$ Proof: From (i) and a well known lemma (gliding principle) midpoints of  $MN, EF$  and  $O_AN_9$  coincide which is enough.

Claim:  $OO_A/2=IF$ .
Proof:  $IF=N_9I-FI=(AH-OO_A)/2-O_AE=OO_A$  by the well known fact  $AH=2OE$ .

Claim:  $F-I_A-O_A$  (or  $O_AI_A$  is perp to  $XY$ )
Proof: By menelause it is enough to prove that  $O_AD/O_AN_9) \cdot (N_9F/FI) \cdot (II_A/I_AD) =1 \iff 2IF=OO_A$ . We used the fact that  $II_A/I_AD=OO_A/O_AD$  because of two similar isosceles triangles.

Now note that  $\angle (O_AI_A;AB)=90-\angle FO_AN=90- \angle AYX=90 -\angle B$  as desired.

<details><summary>sol</summary>Pick the center of  $\odot B'D_BC$ . Let it be called  $O_B$ We can get  $\triangle O_BD_BC\sim\triangle OA'C$  so  $\triangle OO_BC\sim\triangle A'D_BC$ Thus   $$ OO_B^2-O_BC^2={OC^2}\frac{A'D_B^2-D_BC^2}{A'C^2}={OC^2}\frac{\sin^2\angle BCA'-\sin^2\angle D_BA'C}{\sin^2\angle A'D_BC}={OC^2}\frac{\sin(\angle BCA'-\angle D_BA'C)\sin(\angle BCA'+\angle D_BA'C)}{\sin^2\angle A'D_BC}={OC^2}\frac{\sin(\angle BCA'-\angle D_BA'C)}{\sin\angle A'D_BC} $$  But then   $$ \sin(\angle BCA'-\angle D_BA'C)=\sin(90^{\circ}-\angle ACB-\angle D_BA'C)=\sin(\angle D_BM_BC-\angle ACB) $$  So   $$ \frac{\sin(\angle BCA'-\angle D_BA'C)}{\sin\angle A'D_BC}=\frac{\sin \angle D_BM_BC \cos \angle ACB-\sin \angle ACB \cos \angle D_BM_BC}{\sin\angle A'D_BC}=\frac{\sin \angle D_BM_BC}{\sin\angle A'D_BC}\cos \angle ACB-\frac{\sin \angle D_BA'C}{\sin\angle A'D_BC}\sin\angle ACB $$  And then by sine'law or whatever it's called,   $$ \frac{\sin \angle D_BM_BC}{\sin\angle A'D_BC}\cos \angle ACB-\frac{\sin \angle D_BA'C}{\sin\angle A'D_BC}\sin\angle ACB=\frac{D_BC}{M_BC}\cos\angle ACB-\frac{D_BC}{A'C}\sin\angle ACB $$  Let  $OC=OB=R$  ,  $M_BC=kAC$ and write  $\angle ACB= C,\angle ABC=B$ . 
So  $A'C=2R\cos B$ ,  $AC=2R\sin B$ ,  $M_BC=2kR\sin B$ In  $Rt\triangle M_BA'C$ , solve for  $D_BC$  we get  $D_BC=\frac{kR\sin 2B}{(k\sin B\sin C+\cos B\cos C)}$ Plug in we get   $$ \frac{\sin(\angle BCA'-\angle D_BA'C)}{\sin\angle A'D_BC}=\frac{\cos B\cos C -k\sin B\sin C}{k\sin B\sin C+\cos B\cos C} $$  which is symmetric for  $B$  and  $C$ . Thus   $$ OO_B^2-O_BC^2=R^2\frac{\cos B\cos C -k\sin B\sin C}{k\sin B\sin C+\cos B\cos C}=OO_C^2-O_CB^2 $$  So  $O$  is on  $PQ$ .</details>

Here is a proof by PoP Ratio Lemma:

I used  $M$  instead of  $G$ . Let  $r$  be the radius of the circle passing through  $B,C$  with center  $D$ . Let  $R$  be the radius of  $(ABC)$ .  $AH \cap (ABC)=H'$ . Let  $A'$  be the antipode of  $A$  in  $(ABC)$ . Then it is enough to prove that   $$ \frac{FD^2-r^2}{MD^2-r^2}=\frac{FO^2-R^2}{MO^2-R^2} $$  Note that  $FD=HD$ .  $MD^2-r^2=AM^2, FO^2-R^2=FA' \cdot FA, MO^2-R^2=-AM \cdot MD, FD^2-r^2=DH^2-r^2 \overset{Stewart-Theorem} =-HB\cdot HC$ . Thus we want to prove that   $$ HB \cdot HC \cdot \frac{MD}{MA} \overset{?} =FA' \cdot FA=FA'^2+FA' \cdot AA'  $$  Claim:  $HH'=FA'$ Proof: By  $\sqrt{bc}$  inversion, we get  $HAD \sim EAA'$ . Thus  $EA' \parallel HF$ .  $\frac{A'F}{A'G}=\frac{EH}{EG}=\frac{AH}{AG}=\frac{HH'}{GA'}$  as desired. $\square$ Note that the similarity we mentioned earlier gives  $\frac{AD}{AE}= \frac{AD^2}{AD \cdot AE}=\frac{AD^2}{AH \cdot 2R}$ . We just have to prove that   $$ \frac{MD}{MA}=\frac{HH'}{AH}+\frac{2R}{AH} \iff \frac{2AD}{AE}=\frac{HH'}{AH}+\frac{2R}{AH} \iff AD^2=R \cdot AH'+2R $$  By Sin Law  $AH'=2R \cos (B-C)$ . Thus we only have to prove  $2\frac{AD^2}{4R^2}=\cos(B-C)+1 \iff 2\cos^2 (\frac{B-C}{2})=\cos (B-C)+1$  which is true.

Let, $I,I_A, I_B,I_C, I_D$ be the incenters of $ABCD, BCD, CDA, DAB, ABC$ respectively. And let $I_{XY}$ be the incenter of $PXY \ \forall X,Y \in\{A,B,C,D\}$ $\boxed{\textbf{Claim: }I_A, I_B,I_D, I_{BC} \text { are cyclic.}}$ $\underline{\textbf{Proof: }}$ Here, $\measuredangle BAC = \measuredangle BDC \implies \measuredangle BI_DC=\measuredangle BI_AC$ Therefore, $BCI_AI_D$ is also cyclic. As the same, $ADI_BI_C, CDI_AI_B, ABI_CI_D, CAI_BI_D, BDI_AI_C$ are also cyclic. Now let, $\angle BAC = 2\alpha$ . So, $\angle I_{BC}I_DI_B + \angle I_{BC}I_AI_B = \angle I_{BC}I_DI +\angle II_DI_B+\angle I_{BC}I_AI +\angle II_AI_B = 90^\circ - \alpha + \angle IDB + 90^\circ +\angle IDC = 180^\circ - 2\alpha + \angle BDC = 180^\circ$ And we are done. It is now trivial by the claim that all, $I_A,I_B,I_C,I_D, I_{AB}, I_{BC}, I_{CD}, I_{DA}$ lies on the same circle. $\blacksquare$

Solution to P92
Definitions**Definition 1.**Let $c$ refer to isogonal conjugate of $\triangle ABC$ .(For example $cK$ refers to the isogonal conjugate of $K$ WRT $\triangle ABC$ .)**Definition 2.**For four line $l_1,l_2,l_3,l_4$ , define $(l_1,l_2;l_3,l_4)=(l_1',l_2';l_3',l_4')$ , where $l_i'(1\le i\le 4)$ pass the same point and $l_i'\parallel l_i$ .**Definition 3.**We say line $l_1,l_2$ are symmetric with respect to line $l$ , if the symmetry line of $l_1$ WRT $l$ is parallel to or coincide with $l_2$ .**Definition 4.**Define $l_\infty$ the point at infinity on line $l$ .
Let line $PI$ intersect $(O)$ at $U,V$ . Let $\Gamma$ be a hyperbola passing $A,B,C,I,Q$ , then $\Gamma=c(UV)$ . Since $\angle (PI,AI)=\angle (AI,AS)$ , then $S=c(UV_\infty)$ . Thus, $S\in\Gamma$ . Let $l_1,l_2$ be two asymptotes of $\Gamma$ . Then we know $cU=l_1,cV=l_2$ . Since $P$ is the midpoint of segment $UV$ ( $P\in\odot(OI)$ ), we have $$ (AU,AV;AP,UV)=-1. $$ Note that $(AU,l_1)$ , $(AV,l_2)$ , $(AP,AQ)$ , $(UV,AS)$ are symmetric WRT $AI$ respectively. So we have $$ (l_1,l_2;AQ,AS)=(AU,AV;AP,UV)=-1. $$ Then $$ -1=(l_{1\infty},l_{2\infty};Q,S)\stackrel{l_{2\infty}}{=}(l_1,l_2;l_{2\infty}Q,l_{2\infty}S)\implies S,Q \text{ are symmetric WRT }O_0, $$ where $O_0$ is the center of $\Gamma$ . So $O_0$ is the midpoint of $SQ$ . Thus, $S,R,P$ are collinear $\Longleftrightarrow O_0I\parallel SP$ . Let $l_{AV}$ be the symmetry line of $AV$ WRT $AI$ . Then we know $l_{AV}\parallel l_2$ . Now $\angle SUV=180^\circ-\angle SAV=180^\circ -\angle SAI-\angle IAV=180^\circ -\angle AIP-\angle (AI,l_AV)=\angle (UV,l_{AV})$ which gives $SU\parallel l_{AV}\parallel l_2$ . Similarly, $SV\parallel l_1$ . $IP$ intersect $l_2,l_1$ at $X,Y$ , respectively. Note that $IP$ and $\Gamma$ are tangent to point $I$ , then it's well-known that $IX=IY$ . Since $P$ is the midpoint of $UV$ , $SU\parallel O_0X,SV\parallel O_0Y$ , we immediately have $SP\parallel O_0I$ , as desired. $\blacksquare$

**Solution 94:** Let $\omega = \odot(S,SB)$ ; $\Omega = \odot(ABC)$ ; $O$ be center of $\omega$ ; $T$ be antipode of $S$ wrt $\omega$ ; $M$ be the midpoint of segment $PQ$ . Note $PQ$ passes through $O$ .**Claim 1: ** $P,Q$ are isogonal conjugates wrt $\triangle ABC$ . *Proof:* This is because $AP,AQ$ are isogonal wrt $\angle A$ and $\angle BPC + \angle BQC = 180^\circ + \angle A$ . In other words, if $P^*$ is the isogonal conjugate of $P$ wrt $\triangle ABC$ , then $P^* \in AQ$ and $\angle BQC = \angle BPC$ . Hence $P^* \equiv Q$ . An alternate way to see this is: If $I$ is incenter of $\triangle ABC$ , then $IP = IQ$ , so then subtend equal angles on $\omega$ , which implies our Claim. $\square$ **Claim 2: ** $SA_1 = SA_2 = B_1B_2 = C_1C_2$ . *Proof:* Observe that $$ \angle PBQ = \angle PCQ = \frac{\angle PSQ}{2} ~ \textcolor{blue}{\textbf{=}} ~ \frac{\angle PAQ}{2} = \angle SAP = \angle SAQ $$ So arcs $\widehat{SA_1},\widehat{SA_2},\widehat{B_1B_2},\widehat{C_1C_2}$ subtend equal angles on circumference of $\Omega$ , and hence they are equal in length. $\square$ **Claim 3: ** perpendicular bisector of segments $AT,M_2M_3$ coincides, particularly points $A,T,M_2,M_3$ are concyclic. *Proof:* Let $S_2,S_3$ be midpoint of arcs $\widehat{AC},\widehat{AB}$ of $\Omega$ not containing $C,A$ , respectively. Note $O-M_2-S_2$ and $O-M_3-S_3$ . Further, as $B_1B_2 = C_1C_2$ , so $OM_2 = OM_3$ . It follows segments $M_2M_3,S_2S_3$ have same perpendicular bisector. On the other hand, it is well known that segments $S_2S_3,AT$ have same perpendicular bisector. This proves our Claim. $\square$ **(Key) Claim 4: ** $M_3$ is circumcenter of $\triangle AMB$ . Similarly $M_2$ is circumenter of $\triangle AMC$ . *Proof:* Note $B$ is the center of spiral similarity $\sigma$ sending $C_2 \to Q$ and $C_1 \to P$ . Note, $$ \sigma ~:~ M_3 \to M ~~,~~ O \to S $$ So we obtain $$ \triangle BM_3O \sim \triangle BMS \implies \triangle BM_3M \sim \triangle BOS $$ Since $OB = OS$ , thus $M_3B = M_3M$ . Also, $M_3B = M_3A$ . So our Claim is proven. $\square$ It follows that $M_2M_3$ is perpendicular bisector of segment $AM$ . Let $X$ be midpoint of segment $OT$ . It follows (by looking at $S$ ) that $$ \boxed{X \in M_2M_3} $$ Because of **Claim 3**, we just have to show that points $M_1,M_2,M_3,T$ are concylic. Let $\Gamma$ be the circle with center $O$ passing through midpoint of segments $SA_1,SA_2$ . Due to **Claim 2** we obtain $$ M_2,M_3 \in \Gamma $$ Hence it suffices to show $$ \text{Pow}_{\Gamma}(X) = XT \cdot XM_1 $$ Let $Y$ be midpoint of segment $SA_1$ . Observe that \begin{align*} XT \cdot XM_1 &= \frac{XM_1 \cdot XS}{3} = \frac{SX^2 - SM_1 \cdot SX}{3} = \frac{SX^2}{3} - \frac{SM_1 \cdot ST}{4} = \frac{SX^2}{3} - \frac{SA_1^2}{4} = 3OX^2 - SY^2 \text{Pow}_{\Gamma}(X) &= OY^2 - OX^2 = OS^2 - SY^2 - OX^2 = (2OX)^2 - OX^2 - SY^2 = 3OX^2 - SY^2 \end{align*} This completes the proof. $\blacksquare$ **Remark: ** I can't find a synthetic proof for showing $$ \text{Pow}_{\Gamma}(X) = XT \cdot XM_1 $$ One gets that homothety $\mathbb H$ at $S$ at scale factor $2$ sends $\Gamma$ to $\odot(T,TA_1)$ . Problem 101. 
Let  $ABCD$  be a cyclic quadrilateral,  $AC=e$  and  $BD=f.$  Let us denote by  $r_a,r_b,r_c,r_d$  the radii of the incircles of the triangles  $BCD,CDA,DAB,ABC,$  respectively. Prove that  $e\cdot r_a\cdot r_c=f\cdot r_b\cdot r_d.$

Let  $a,b,c,d$  denote the lengths of  $AB,BC,CD,DA$ .
Let  $R$  be the circumradius of  $ABCD$ .  $$ r_A=\frac{abf}{2R(a+b+f)} $$    $$ r_C=\frac{cdf}{2R(c+d+f)} $$    $$ r_B=\frac{bcf}{2R(b+c+e)} $$    $$ r_D=\frac{adf}{2R(a+d+e)} $$  Now seeing at what we need to prove it's equivalent to showing-  $$ \frac{f}{(a+b+f)(c+d+f)}=\frac{e}{(c+b+e)(a+d+e)} $$  or,  $$ f(ab+cd)=e(ad+bc) $$  Now area of ABCD $=\frac{1}{2}(ab+cd)\sin \angle DAB=\frac{1}{2}(ad+bc)\sin \angle ABC$   $$ \implies \frac{ab+cd}{ad+bc}=\frac{\sin \angle ABC}{\sin \angle DAB}=\frac{e/2R}{f/2R}=\frac{e}{f} $$   as desired

<details><summary>Solution 110</summary>Well, with complex numbers and around an hour, the problem is done.
But here's my synthetic approach:

Let  $O, H$  be the circumcenter and orthocenter of  $ABC$  and  $O', H'$  be the circumcenter and orthocenter of  $AEF$ .

Let  $Y, Z$  be the intersections of lines  $FH, OM$  and  $NH, OE$ .
Let  $Y', Z'$  be the intersections of lines  $EH', O'N$  and  $MH', O'F$ .

By Desargues Theorem, we only have to prove that  $A, Y, Z$  are collinear and  $A, Y', Z'$  are collinear. (It's totally analogous but anyway)

Let  $X$  be the intersection of lines  $EH, ON$  and let  $X'$  be the intersection of lines  $FH', O'M$ .

Let  $D$  be the midpoint of  $AX$  and  $D'$  be the midpoint of  $AX'$ .
Let  $U, V$  be the midpoints of  $NE, MF$ .
Let  $K, K'$  be the midpoints of  $OH, O'H'$ .
Let  $W, W'$  be the midpoints of  $XZ, XZ'$ .

Then we see the newton-gauss line generated by the quadrilateral formed from the lines  $HX, XO, OZ, ZH$  so  $U, K, W$  are collinear.

But we know that  $K$  is the center of the nine-point circle of  $ABC$  so  $K$  lies on the perpendicular bisector of segment  $NE$  which implies that  $D, U, K$  are collinear since  $N, E$  are on  $(AX)$  and  $U$  is the midpoint of  $NE$ .

Also,  $HX \| OY$  and  $XO \| YH$  so  $K$  is the midpoint of  $XY$ .
Hence, by duplicating (homothety) the line  $D, K, W$  over the point  $X$  we conclude that  $A, Y, Z$  are collinear.

The rest is similar:  $H'X' \| O'Y'$  and  $X'O' \| Y'H'$  so  $K'$  is the midpoint of  $X'Y'$ .

Then we see the newton-gauss line generated by the quadrilateral formed from the lines  $H'X', X'O', O'Z', Z'H'$  so  $V, K', W'$  are collinear.

Let  $E', F'$  be the intersections of  $FH', AE$  and  $MO', AF$ .

But we know that  $K'$  is the center of the nine-point circle of  $AEF$  so  $K'$  lies on the perpendicular bisector of segment  $E'F'$  which implies that  $D', V, K'$  are collinear since  $E', F'$  are on  $(FM)$  and on  $(AX')$ .

Hence, by duplicating the line  $D', K', W'$  over the point  $X'$  we conclude that  $A, Y', Z'$  are collinear. We are done!</details>

<details><summary>Solution 114</summary>Denote the three circles  $\omega_A$ ,  $\omega_B$  and  $\omega_C$ . Let  $\Omega$  be the circle internally tangent to  $\omega_A$ ,  $\omega_B$  and  $\omega_C$ .

This implies that the external  tangents to  $\omega_A$  and  $\Omega$  passes through  $A$ . Similarly,  $B$  is the exsimilicenter  $\omega_B$  and  $\Omega$  and  $C$  is the exsimilicenter  $\omega_C$  and  $\Omega$ . 

By Monge's theorem on  $\Omega$ ,  $\omega_B$  and  $\omega_C$ , the exsimilicenter of  $\omega_B$  and  $\omega_C$  lies on  $BC$ , but it also lies on  $O_BO_C$  so  $BC\cap O_BO_C$  is the exsimilicenter of  $\omega_B$  and  $\omega_C$ . Similarly,  $CA\cap O_CO_A$  is the exsimilicenter of  $\omega_A$  and  $\omega_C$  and  $AB\cap O_AO_B$  is the exsimilicenter of  $\omega_A$  and  $\omega_B$ .

By Monge's theorem on  $\omega_A$ ,  $\omega_B$  and  $\omega_C$  we get  $BC\cap O_BO_C$ ,  $CA\cap O_CO_A$  and  $AB\cap O_AO_B$  so by Desargues perspective theorem we are done.</details>

<details><summary>sol129</summary>We will prove that  $(AKL)$ ,  $(A_1B_1C_1)$  and  $(DEA_1)$  share two points.

Let  $M$  be the midpoint of  $BC$ . Since  $(A_1B_1C_1)$   is the NPC we have  $M\in(A_1B_1C_1)$ . 

Note that  $MK\parallel CC_1$  and  $ML\parallel BB_1$  we have  $\angle KML=180^{\circ}-\angle KMB-\angle CML=180^{\circ}-\angle C_1CB-\angle CBB_1=180^{\circ}-\angle A$  so  $M\in(AKL)$ Since  $\bigtriangleup BA_1C_1\cup K\sim\bigtriangleup B_1A_1C\cup L$  we have  $\angle KA_1L=180^{\circ}-\angle KA_1B-\angle CA_1L=180^{\circ}-\angle KA_1B-\angle C_1A_1K=180^{\circ}-\angle A$  hence  $A_1\in(AKL)$ .

Now we will prove that  $M\in(DEA_1)$ . Since  $\angle AA_1D=90^{\circ}-DA_1B=90^{\circ}-\angle DAB=90^{\circ}-\angle CAE=90^{\circ}-\angle CA_1E=\angle EA_1A$  so  $A_1A$  is the angle bisector in  $\angle DA_1E$ . But since  $AA_1\perp BC$ , we get  $BC$  is the external angle bisector of  $\angle DA_1E$ . Hence it suffices to show that  $M$  is on the perpendicular bisector of  $DE$ . 

Let  $P=AD\cap (AC)\neq A$ ,  $Q=AE\cap (AB)\neq A$ . We may angle chase to get  $DEQP$  cyclic. Now note that  $\angle PAC_1=\angle CAE$  so  $PE\parallel CC_1$ . So the perpendicular bisector of  $PE$  is the perpendicular bisector of  $CC_1$  which passes through  $M$ . Similarly, the perpendicular bisector of  $DQ$  passes through  $M$ , so  $M$  is the center of  $DEQP$ . Now this implies that  $M$  lies on the perpendicular bisector of  $DE$ , and we are done.</details>

Observe that by Pascal on $E'TF'BAC$ and then Desargues perspective theorem on $\bigtriangleup BFF'$ and $\bigtriangleup E'EC$ gives $BE'$ , $CF'$ and $EF$ concurrent. We conclude that $BE'\parallel CF'\parallel AG\parallel XY$ . Now assume that $PT$ bisects angle $BTE$ and let $PT$ intersect $(ABC)$ at $M\neq T$ . Then $M$ is the midpoint of arcs $BE', CF', AG, XY$ . It is not hard to prove that $GY$ is tangent to $(CEY)$ so we must prove that $D$ , $G$ and $Y$ are colinear. By DDIT on $\mathcal{Q}\{BC,CX,XY,YB\}$ there is an involution swapping $$ (TB,TX), (TC,TY), (TD,TP) $$ Projecting through $T$ onto $(ABC)$ we get an involution swapping $$ (B,X),(C,Y),(G,M) $$ and projecting through the point at infinity along $XY$ , we get $$ (E',Y),(F',X),(A,M) $$ so $M$ , $G$ and $Q$ are colinear and $M$ , $A$ and $R$ are colinear. By symmetry in construction of $Q$ and $R$ , $QR$ is parallel to $XY$ , hence $X_1$ , $Q$ and $R$ are colinear. Angle chase to get $X_1XAR$ cyclic and then chase to get $X_1ME'R$ cyclic. Let  $c$  be the circumconic of  $ABC$  which is isogonal conjugate of  $GD$ . Clearly  $K \in c$ . Since isogonal conjugate of  $D$  is  $A$  and isogonal of  $AD$  is line through  $A$  parallel to  $BC$  so the line through  $A$  parallel to  $BC$  is tangent to  $c$ . Now note that polar of  $\infty_{BC}$  is  $A$ -median. Let  $\infty _{BC}K \cap c=K,E''$ . Since polar of  $\infty_{BC}$  is  $AM$  so midpoint of  $KE''$  lie on  $AM$  implying that  $AK, AE''$  are isotomic. Hence  $E''=E'$ . Hence  $E'$  is isogonal conjugate of  $E$ .Let  $Q$  be the reflection of  $E$  across  $M$ . From parallelogram isogonality lemma we know that  $A-E'-R'-Q$  are collinear. We begin with proving $AO_C\parallel CO_A$ . Note that $$ \angle(O_CA,AC)=\angle O_CAB-\angle BAC=\frac{\pi}{2}-\angle ADB-\angle BAC $$ and $$ \angle(O_AC,AC)=\angle BCA-\angle O_ACB=\angle BCA-(\frac{\pi}{2}-\angle CDB)=\angle BCA+\angle CDB-\frac{\pi}{2} $$ so it suffices to show that $$ \angle BCA+\angle CDB+\angle ADB+\angle BAC=\pi $$ But this is indeed true since $\angle CDB+\angle ADB=\angle ADC=\angle ABC$ and using the fact that the angle sum in a triangle is $\pi$ . Now we have $$ \frac{BO_A}{BO_C}=\frac{CO_A}{AO_C}=\frac{O_AY}{O_CY} $$ so by the angle bisector theorem, we are done.**Claim.** $O_B$ and $H$ are isogonal conjugates in $\bigtriangleup XGO_A$ and $\bigtriangleup XFO_C$ .**Proof.** Firstly, $$ \angle GXH=\frac{1}{2}\angle BXE=\angle BDE=\frac{1}{2}\pi-\angle(BD,\overline{O_AO_CX})=\angle(XO_B,\overline{O_AO_CX})=\angle O_BXD $$ so $XH$ and $XO_B$ are isogonal in $\angle GXO_A=\angle FXO_C$ . Given triangle $ABC$ , $Q$ is a point on $(ABC)$ . $D$ is a point s.t. $BD\perp BC$ , $E_1$ is a point on $AD$ s.t. $BE_1//AC$ . $E$ is the reflection of $E'$ over $BD$ , $E_2$ is the reflection of $E$ over $BQ$ . Let the perpendicular bisector of $BC$ intersect $AD$ at $P$ . $R$ lies on $BQ$ s.t. $PQ// DR$ . Prove that $A,E_2,R$ are collinear.
Pf: We fix $A,B,C,Q$ , and let $D$ be a varying point on the line passing through $B$ perpendicular to $BC$ . Then $D\mapsto AD\mapsto E_1\mapsto E\mapsto E_2$ is projective. Also $D\mapsto AD\mapsto P\mapsto \infty_{PQ}$ is projective. When $D=\infty_{\perp BC}$ , $P=\infty_{PQ}=\infty_{\perp BC}$ where $\infty_{\perp BC}$ is the direction perpendicular to $BC$ . So $D\infty{PQ}$ passes through a fixed point, $D\mapsto D\infty_{PQ}\mapsto R$ is projective. Therefore $E_2\mapsto R$ is projective, and it suffices to check for the collinearity of $A,E_2,R$ for three cases. (since $E_2\mapsto AE_2\cap BQ$ is projective) When $D=B$ , $E_1=E=E_2=R=B$ , so $A,E_2,R$ are collinear. When $D$ lies on $AQ$ , then $P,R$ lies on $AQ$ . $E_1$ lies on $AQ$ s.t. $E_1B//AC$ . $E_2$ satisfies $E_1B=E_2B$ and $\measuredangle E_1BE_2=2\measuredangle DBQ$ , and it suffices to prove that $E_2$ lies on $AQ$ . Let the foot from $B$ to $AQ$ be $H$ , then $\measuredangle HBE_1=90^\circ+\measuredangle HE_1B=90^\circ+\measuredangle QAC=\measuredangle CBD+\measuredangle QBC=\measuredangle QBD$ . Therefore $E_2$ is the reflection of $E_1$ wrt $BH$ , which lies on $AQ$ , so $AQE_2R$ are collinear. When $D$ lies on $AC$ , then $E_1,E,E_2$ lies on $\ell_\infty$ . Let $\ell_2=BE_2$ , $\ell_1=BE_1$ . Then $\measuredangle(\ell_1,\ell_2)=2\measuredangle DBQ$ . We have $P$ is on $AC$ , $RD//PQ$ . Let $F$ be the intersection of the perpendicular bisector of $BC$ and $BQ$ , $G=BQ\cap AC$ . Then $GF/GB=GP/GD=GQ/GR$ (since $BD//FP, DR//PQ$ ), so $GF\cdot GR=GB\cdot GQ=GA\cdot GC$ , $F,R,A,C$ are concyclic. $\measuredangle RAC=\measuredangle RFC=\measuredangle BFC=2\measuredangle BFP=2\measuredangle QBD= \measuredangle(\ell_2,\ell_1)=\measuredangle (\ell_2, AC)$ Therefore $\ell_2//AR$ , $E_2=\infty_{\ell_2}$ lies on $AR$ . So $A,R,E_2$ are always collinear, i.e. $\angle ARB=\angle ERB$ as desired.

This is one of the nicest geo problems I've seen in a while tbh. Let $K$ and $L$ be the tangential points of $(I)$ and $BC$ , $EF$ respectively. Let $H$ be the orthocenter of $ABC$ . By Brianchon's theorem, we have $K, H, L$ collinear. We prove that $HK$ bisects $\angle BHC$ .
ProofWe use the law of sines. Observe that \[\frac{BK}{KC} = \frac{\sin \angle BIK}{\sin \angle IBK} \cdot \frac{\sin \angle ICK}{\sin \angle CIK} = \frac{\sin \angle LEI}{\sin \angle EIL} \cdot \frac{\sin \angle FIL}{\sin \angle LFI} = \frac{FL}{LE}\] On the other hand, we have \[\frac{\sin \angle BHK}{\sin \angle HBK} \cdot \frac{\sin \angle HCK}{\sin \angle CHK} = \frac{BK}{CK} =\frac{FL}{LE} = \frac{\sin \angle FHL}{\sin \angle LFH} \cdot \frac{\sin \angle LEH}{\sin \angle LHE}\] This implies that $\frac{\sin \angle BHK}{\sin \angle CHK} = \frac{\sin \angle FHL}{ \sin \angle LHE} = \frac{\sin \angle CHK}{\sin \angle BHK}$ and hence $\angle BHK = \angle CHK$ . $\square$
Let $O$ be the circumcenter of $ABC$ . Let $Q$ be the tangential point of the $A$ -excircle and $BC$ . We prove that $I, O, Q$ collinear.
ProofLet $N$ be the midpoint of $BC$ . It is well known that $BK = QC$ so we have $KN=NQ$ . Therefore, it actually suffices to show that $2ON=IK$ . Recall that $\angle BHK = \angle CHK$ . This implies that $AI \parallel HK$ by simple angle chasing. Hence, $AIKH$ is a parallelogram. In particular, we have $AH = IK$ . Now we use the law of sines. Notice that \[2ON = BC \cdot \frac{\sin (90 - \angle A)}{\sin \angle A} = \frac{BC}{\sin 90} \cdot \frac{\sin \angle FBE}{\sin A} = \frac{EF}{\sin \angle A} = AH = IK\] Hence, we are done. $\square$
Now we are finally well equipped to show that $GI$ bisects $\angle BGC$ .
ProofLet $AI$ intersect $(ABC)$ at $M$ . Let $S$ be the projection of $I$ onto $AD$ . It is well known that $S, K, M$ are collinear. It follows that $\triangle IDK = \triangle SDK \sim \triangle KNM = \triangle QNM$ and hence $\angle IDK = \angle MQN$ which implies that $ID \parallel QM$ . Let $P$ be the midpoint of $GM$ . Obviously, $OP \perp GM$ . Since we also have $IO = OQ$ , $OP \parallel IG \parallel QM$ which implies that $IG \perp GM$ . Therefore, $\angle BGI = 90 - \angle BCM = 90 - \angle CBM = \angle IGC$ . $\square$
Now we just bash to finish. Let $AG$ intersect $EF$ at $L'$ . Note that the previous claim implies $\frac{BG}{GC} = \frac{BD}{DC}$ . Therefore, by the law of sines we have \[\frac{FL'}{L'E} = \frac{\sin \angle FAL'}{\sin \angle AFL'} \cdot \frac{\sin \angle FEL'}{\sin \angle EAL'} = \frac{BD}{DC} \cdot \frac{\sin \angle B}{\sin \angle C} = \frac{\sin(90-\angle B)}{\sin (90 - \angle C)} = \frac{FH}{HE} = \frac{FL}{LE}\] It follows that $L' = L$ $\blacksquare$

P183:In an acute-angled, non-isosceles triangle \(ABC\) with \(\angle A \neq 60^\circ\) and an inscribed circle \((O)\), assuming \((O), B, \text{ and } C\) are fixed while \(A\) varies, let \(D, E, \text{ and } F\) be the projections of \(A, B, \text{ and } C\) onto \(BC, CA, \text{ and } AB\), respectively. \(H\) is the orthocenter of \(\triangle ABC\), and \(I\) is the midpoint of \(OH\). The intersections of \(DE\) and \(DF\) with \(AC\) and \(AB\) are denoted as \(M\) and \(N\), respectively. Define \(J\) as the symmetric point of \(I\) with respect to \(MN\). Prove that \(J\) lies on a fixed circle. ( This problem from Tran Minh Ngoc )

<details><summary>Solution #183</summary>We rename  $I$  to be  $N$ , and  $M$ ,  $N$  og  $X$ , and  $Y$  respectively, and also rename  $J$  to be  $R$ . We define the intersection of  $OH$  and  $XY$  to be  $K$ . 
It is well-known that the line  $XK$  is the radical-axis of  $(ABC)$  and  $(N)$ . 
Therefore,  $$ KO^2 - R^2 = KN^2- \frac{R^2}{4} \Leftrightarrow \frac{3R^2}{4} = KO^2-KN^2=(KO+KN)(KO-KN)=OR \cdot ON. $$  Therefore,  $N$  and  $R$  swap under the inversion with center  $O$  and  $r^2=\frac{3R^2}{4}$ .
Thus,  $R$  moves on a circle iff  $N$  moves on a circle. 
We know that  $N$  moves on a circle iff  $H$  moves on a circle, since  $N$  is the midpoint of  $OH$ , But  $H$  moves on a circle, since  $\angle BHC=180-\angle A$  which is constant by the question statement.</details>

<details><summary>Problem #184</summary>Let  $\mathcal{K}$  be a cubic curve and  $P$  be a point. Prove that there exist six (possibly complex) tangents to  $\mathcal{K}$  that pass through  $P$ , and that these tangency points lie on a conic.</details>

<details><summary>Solution 184</summary>Let  $\mathcal{C}$  be a curve of degree n and  $P$  be a point. By the definition of [polar curve](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_curve), the tangents from  $P$  to  $\mathcal{C}$  lie on a curve of degree n-1. Hence by [Bézout's theorem](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9zout%27s_theorem) there are at most n(n-1) such tangency points.  $\blacksquare$</details>

**This is LoloChen's approach to <u>Problem 189</u>**


Here's a solution using linearity of PoP.
Let the exterior, interior angle bisector of  $\angle EDF$  intersects  $EF$  at  $G, H$  respectively. Let  $\odot ABC, \odot WNX$  and  $\odot YMZ$  be  $c, c_1, c_2$  respectively. Let the radical axis of  ${c}$  and  $c_1$  cut  $YZ$  at  ${K}$  and that of  ${c}$  and  $c_2$  cut  $WX$  at  ${J}$ . We denote the nine point circle of  $\triangle ABC$  as  $c_9$ . Let  $MN\cap EF=I$ , and the in/ex-bisector of  $\angle BAC$  cut  $BC$  at  $P,Q$ resp. For any point  ${V}$  and  $i \in \left\{ 1, 2, 9 \right\} $  define  $f_i(V)=Pow(V , c_i)-Pow(V, c)$ . To prove  $\odot ABC, \odot WNX$  and  $\odot YMZ$  has a common point, we only need  $NJ \perp MK$ . 

It's easily shown that  $f_1(D)=\frac{a^2-bc}{4}$  and  $f_2(D)=\frac{a^2+bc}{4}$  by the properties of incenter and excenter. Moreover,  $YZEF, XWEF$  are concyclic respectively, so  $Pow(G , c_1)=Pow(G , c_9)$  and  $Pow(H , c_2)=Pow(H , c_9)$ , so  $f_1(G)=f_9(G)$  and  $f_2(H)=f_9(H)$ . Since  $\frac{\overline{FG}}{\overline{EG}}=-\frac{b}{c}$  and  $\frac{\overline{FH}}{\overline{EH}}=\frac{b}{c}$ ,   $$ f_1(G)=f_9(G)=\frac{b}{b-c}f_9(E)+\frac{-c}{b-c}f_9(F)=\frac{b}{b-c}\frac{b^2}{4}+\frac{-c}{b-c}\frac{c^2}{4}=\frac{b^2+bc+c^2}{4} $$    $$ f_2(H)=f_9(H)=\frac{b}{b+c}f_9(E)+\frac{c}{b+c}f_9(F)=\frac{b}{b+c}\frac{b^2}{4}+\frac{c}{b+c}\frac{c^2}{4}=\frac{b^2-bc+c^2}{4} $$  Now we can compute  $\frac{\overline{KD}}{\overline{DG}}=\frac{f_1(D)-0}{f_1(G)-f_1(D)}=\frac{a^2-bc}{(b+c-a)(b+c+a)}$ , and the respective  $\frac{\overline{JD}}{\overline{DH}}=\frac{a^2+bc}{(-b+c-a)(-b+c+a)}$ .
The next step is rotate and scale  $\triangle JDN$  such that  $JDN$  becomes  $J'DM$ ; we would like to prove  $KDJ'M$  concyclic, which gives us  $KM\perp JN$  as desired. By ptolemy it is   $$ KD\sin\angle MDJ'+DJ'\sin\angle KDM=DM\sin\angle KDJ'=DM $$  Notice  $90-\angle KDM=\angle MDJ'=\angle NDJ=\angle HGD$ . We have  $\sin\angle HGD=\frac{DI}{DG}$  so we have a  $\frac{KD}{DG}$  term; similarly  $\frac{JD}{DH}$ . By dividing  $DM$  at both sides this equality turns into one involving only the basic lengths of  $\triangle ABC$ , which is then obvious.

This problem has two main roadblocks: 1. the weird condition of where $T$ is, and 2. the weird $\angle NHT$ . We will deal with these first.
Part 1: Dealing with BDH and TDOLet $DT$ intersect $AC$ at $K$ . Note that $H$ and $O$ are isogonal conjugates of $ABDK$ . We use a well-known lemma (See [ISL 2008 G6](https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h287868p30832453)) that state that if $X$ has a isogonal conjugate, then the feet of the altitude from $X$ to the sides are concyclic and that $\angle AXB+\angle CXD=180^\circ$ . Indeed, we can apply our lemma to get that the foot of the altitude of $H$ on $DT$ is on the nine-point circle. Take the homothety at $H$ with factor $2$ . This takes the nine-point circle to the circumcircle and takes the foot of altitude to $H'$ , the reflection of $H$ across $DT$ . This means that $H'$ is on $(ABC)$ . Our other part of the lemma states that $\angle DHK=180^\circ-\angle AHB=\angle KCD$ so $H'$ is also on $(CKD)$ .
Part 2: Dissecting THNWe have \[\angle THN=\angle NHD-\angle THD=\angle NDC-\angle TH'D\] Note that $\angle NDC-\angle ABN=\angle AND$ due to equal arcs $BN$ and $CN$ . Therefore, it suffices to show that $\angle AND=\angle TH'D$ which is equivalent to $NTH'D$ cyclic.
We have gotten rid of the roadblocks and made all the definitions involved in our problem much more easier
Part 3: Finish\[\angle TDH'=\angle KDH'=\angle KCH'=\angle ACH'=180^\circ-\angle ANH'=\angle TNH'\] we are done

**Solution** (maybe overkill): Let $P_1$ be the $P$ -antipode in triangle $ADP$ . Define $Q_1$ , $R_1$ , $S_1$ similarly. By Reflecting in the midpoint of $AD$ , the conclusion is equivalent with $P_1Q_1R_1S_1$ being cyclic. Let $K$ be the reflection of $H$ in $BC$ . Then the points $U$ and $V$ can be defined as the intersections of a circle tangent to $(ABC)$ at $K$ with $BC$ . Now, invert in $A$ to get the following **Equivalent problem**: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with diameter $AD$ . $K=BC\cap AD$ . A circle tangent to $BC$ at $K$ intersects $(ABC)$ at $U$ and $V$ . A circle through $A$ and $U$ intersects $BC$ at $P$ and $Q$ . Another circle through $A$ and $U$ intersects $BC$ at $R$ and $S$ . $P_1$ is the intersection of $DP$ and the line perpendicular to $AP$ through $A$ . Define $Q_1$ , $R_1$ , and $S_1$ similarly. Prove $P_1Q_1R_1S_1$ cyclic. Let $L$ be on $\Omega:=(ABC)$ s.t. $AL\perp BC$ .**Claim**: $P_1$ and so on lie on a circumhyperbola of $\bigtriangleup ALD$ tangent to $\Omega$ at $A$ .**Proof**. Consider the Maps $P\mapsto DP$ and $P\mapsto AP\overset{\perp}{\mapsto}AP^{\perp,A} $ are of degree 1, so $P_1=DP\cap AP^{\perp,A} $ is of degree $2$ , hence on conic, $c$ . For $P\in\{\infty_{BC},K,BC\cap AA\}$ , we get $L$ , $A$ , and $D$ on the conic. When $P=B$ we get $P_1=\infty_{BD}$ . Takling isogonal conjugation wrt. $ADL$ , we find that the $C$ -antipode in $\Omega$ lies on the isogonal image of $c$ . Similarly for $P=C$ . Thus the isogonal image of $c$ is parallel to $LD$ and intersects $(ADL)$ - i.e. $c$ is tangent to $\Omega$ at $A$ and is a hyperbola.**Note**: $UV$ passes through a fixed point; indeed, just consider radical axis theorem on $\Omega$ , $(KUV)$ and a circle tangent to $BC$ at $K$ and tangent to $\Omega$ .**Claim**. For fixed $U$ (and thus $V$ ), the points $\infty_{P_1Q_1}$ and $\infty_{R_1S_1}$ are fixed.**Proof**. By DIT on $AUIJ$ where $I$ and $J$ are the circle points, we find an involution swapping $(P,Q)$ on line $BC$ . Projecting onto $c$ through $D$ , thus involution swaps $(P_1,Q_1)$ , and thus $P_1Q_1$ pass through a fixed point. It swaps in particular $(B,C)$ and thus on $c$ , $(c\cap DB,c\cap DC)$ - i.e. The points at inifnity on $c$ . Hence the fixed point must be a point on the line at infinity, so all $P_1Q_1$ are parallel as claimed. Similarly, this holds for $R_1S_1$ . By generalized Reim, it suffices to find, for a given pair of $U$ and $V$ , one particular case where $P_1Q_1R_1S_1$ is cyclic. Indeed, the following suffices: Let the lines parallel to $P_1Q_1$ and $R_1S_1$ through $A$ $c$ at $X$ and $Y$ . Then prove $(AXY)$ is tangent to $c$ . Equivalently, tangent to $\Omega$ , and thus isogonal in $\angle A$ . **Claim**. When $U$ (and thus $V$ ) moves on $\Omega$ , $A\infty_{P_1Q_1}$ and $A\infty_{R_1S_1}$ are isogonal. Proof. We easily get $A\infty_{P_1Q_1}$ and $A\infty_{R_1S_1}$ move of degree $1$ . Then to get “ $Z=\Omega\cap A\infty_{P_1Q_1}$ , $W=\Omega\cap A\infty_{R_1S_1}$ , and $\infty_{BC}$ are colinear”, we need to check $1+1+0+1=3$ cases. 1. $U=B$ and thus $V=C$ : Then we find $\{Z,W\}= \{B,C\}$ -antipodes. 2. $U=C$ and thus $V=B$ : Similar to above. 3. $U=D$ : We find for $P=K$ , that $\infty_{P_1Q_1}= \infty_{BC^\perp}$ , and for $R=AA\cap BC$ , that $\infty_{R_1S_1}= \infty_{AD}$ . Hence $\{Z,W\}= \{K,L\}$ which suffices. We finally conclude the problem. Next, as above:

Denote the midpoint of $BC$ as $M$ , $A_1=BC\cap AK_A$ , $S=BC\cap K_BK_C$ , $T$ the intersection of tangents to $\omega$ at $B$ and $C$ . We easily find $AOMK_ADS$ cyclic with diameter $OS$ and $SA$ tangent to $\omega$ . By radax, $DX$ pass through $S$ . Then $$ (D,L;A,\infty_AK)\overset{S}{=}(X,O;A,S)\overset{M}{=}(K,T;A,A_1)\overset{well-known}{=}-1. $$ This yields the claim. The above claim gives $\Gamma=(O,2R)$ . The proof also implies that $OX\cap AK$ is the midpoint of $AL$ . Then we have: \[ k = \frac{a^2(c-1)^2 + c}{a^2c + 1}. \] Let $L$ be the intersection of $AN$ and $BM$ , which gives: \[ l = \frac{2a^2 - a^2c + c}{a^2 + 1}. \] Let $T$ be the reflection of $B$ about $AN$ . Аfter polar duality wrt the incircle the problem transforms to following statement:**Transformed problem:**Triangle $ABC$ inscribed in circle $\Omega$ with center $O$ and circumscribed around ellipse $\mathcal{E}$ with foci $F_1$ and $F_2$ , such that $O \in F_1F_2$ . Let $l$ be the tangent line to $\mathcal{E}$ which is parallel to $BC$ , and $m_1$ , $m_2$ be the tangent lines to $\mathcal{E}$ which are perpendicular to $F_1F_2$ . Let $l$ intersects $m_1$ , $m_2$ at points $P$ , $Q$ . Then $AP \perp AQ$ .**Lemma:** Points $F_1$ , $F_2$ lie on the circle with diameter $PQ$ .
Proof of the lemmaLet $m_1$ tangents $\mathcal{E}$ at $K$ . Points $L$ and $M$ are the reflections of $F_2$ around $m_1$ and $l$ respectively. Then $F_1M = 2a = F_1K+F_2K = F_1L$ ( $2a$ is the major axis of $\mathcal{E}$ ) and $PM=PF_2=PL$ $\implies$ triangles $\Delta F_1PM$ and $\Delta F_1PL$ are equal, so $F_1P$ is the angle bisector of $\angle MF_1L$ . $P$ lies on the perpendicular bisector to $MF_2$ and $PM \neq PF_2$ , therefore, $P \in (F_1MF_2)$ . Similary, $Q \in (F_1MF_2)$ , and the center of $(MPQF_1F_2)$ lies on $l$ , so we are done.
*Remark:* The lemma doesn't involve $\Delta ABC$ and its properties. So it could be reformulated for an arbitary ellipse. After using lemma, it's enough to prove that the circumcenter of $\Delta AF_1F_2$ also lies on $l$ . Let $l$ intersects $(ABC)$ at points $X$ , $Y$ and intersects segments $AB$ , $AC$ at points $C'$ , $B'$ respectively. Consider composition $\varphi$ of inversion with center $A$ and radius $\sqrt{AB \cdot AB'} = \sqrt{AC \cdot AC'}$ and reflection around the internal angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ . It is clear that $\varphi$ swaps $(B, B')$ , $(C, C')$ . Consequently, it swaps $(\Omega, l)$ . Since $\varphi$ is the particular case of the Clawson conjugation, it swaps $F_1, F_2$ . Then, $\varphi$ maps the circumcenter of $(AF_1F_2)$ to the reflection of $A$ wrt $F_1F_2$ , so one needs to show that this reflection lies on $\Omega$ , but it is obviously true because $O \in F_1F_2$ .

S214Lemma 1: The point $P$ lies on ray $OI$ with $IP:OP = r:2R$ , where $r$ , $R$ are the inradius and circumradius respectively. Proof:Take a homothety with ratio $0.5$ at $I$ of the intouch triangle. Then it suffices to prove that $P$ is the exsimilicenter of this homothetied triangle and the medial triangle of the excentral triangle. Consider the $B$ - and $C$ - mixtilinear incircles $\omega _B$ and $\omega _ C$ . We have that the south pole lies on the radical axis of $\omega _B$ and $\omega _ C$ by the shooting lemma. Additionally, the midpoint of $ID$ lies on the radical axis by a simple application of linpop and Pythagoras, hence the radical axis of $\omega _B$ and $\omega _ C$ passes through the desired exsimilicenter. By symmetry, we find that $P$ is the desired point. Lemma 2:Let T be the insimilicenter of the incircle and the circumcircle and $J$ the inverse of $J$ wrt the circumcircle, then we have $$ (J, I; P, T) = -1 $$ . Proof: This is a length chase, recall that $OI = \sqrt{R^2 - 2rR}$ , and $OJ= \frac{R^2}{OI}$ . We also have $\frac{OT}{TI} = \frac{R}{r}$ , so $OT = \frac{R}{r+R} OI$ . We also have $OP = \frac{2R}{2R-r} OI$ . Hence $$ \frac{JP}{IP} = \frac{JO - PO}{PO - IO} = \frac{\frac{R^2}{R^2 - 2rR} - \frac{2R}{2R-r}}{\frac{2R}{2R-r}-1} = \frac{2R^3 - rR^2 - 2R^3 + 4r R^2}{rR(R-2r)} = \frac{3R}{(R-2r)}. $$ and $$ \frac{JT}{IT} = \frac{JO - TO}{IO - TO} = \frac{\frac{R^2}{R^2-2rR} - \frac{R}{r+R}}{1- \frac{R}{r+R}} = \frac{R^2r + R^3 - R^3 + 2rR^2 }{rR(R-2r)}=\frac{3R}{R-2r}. $$ Now we are ready for the problem. Consider an isogonal conjugation, which preserves cross ratios. Then $I$ is fixed and $J$ is sent to the antipode $K$ of $I$ on the Feuerbach hyperbola (proof: let $OI$ intersect the circumcircle at $X$ , $Y$ Then $-1=(X,Y;I,J)=(X', Y';I, K)$ and $X'$ , $Y'$ are the points at infinity of the hyperbola). The point $T$ is sent to the Gergonne point $G$ (proof: Monge + mixtilinear properties). Finally $P$ is sent to $Q$ by definition. Now since $J$ , $I$ , $P$ , $T$ lie on $OI$ with $(J, I; P, T) = -1$ , we have $K$ , $G$ , $Q$ , $I$ lie on the Feuerbach hyperbola with $(K, I; Q, G) = -1$ . However, as the tangents to the hyperbola are parallel to $OI$ (they are antipodes and $IO$ is tangent at $I$ ), we find that $QG$ is parallel to $OI$ .

stem_md:
Given an integer \( n \geq 2024 \). Let \( S_n = \{\sigma_1, \sigma_2, \cdots, \sigma_m\} \) be the set of all \( m = n! \) permutations of \(\{1, 2, \cdots, n\}\). For \(\sigma, \tau \in S_n\), define \( v(\sigma, \tau) \) as the number of elements in
\[\{(i, j) | 1 \leq i < j \leq n, (\sigma(i) - \sigma(j)) (\tau(i) - \tau(j)) < 0\}.\]
Let
\[S = \sum_{i=1}^m v(\sigma_i, \sigma_{i+1}),\]
where \(\sigma_{m+1} = \sigma_1\). Determine the maximum possible value of \( S \). 

*Proposed by Xianbang Wang, High School Affiliated to Renmin University of China*
solution_md:
Answer.  ${n!(n^2 - n - 1)}/{2}$ . 

The maximum value of \( v(\sigma, \tau) \) is \( \frac{n(n-1)}{2} \), and equality holds if and only if \( \sigma \) and \( \tau \) are reverse permutations. Therefore, the number of cases achieving equality is at most half, i.e., \( \frac{m}{2} \) pairs; for the remaining pairs, \( v \leq \frac{n(n-1)}{2} - 1 \). Summing these up yields our result.

For the construction, we prove that such a construction exists for all \( n \geq 4 \). First, consider pairing mutually reverse permutations \( (\sigma, \text{reverse}(\sigma)) \) such that they must be adjacent in the construction. To connect pairs \( (\sigma, \text{reverse}(\sigma)) \) and \( (\sigma', \text{reverse}(\sigma')) \), it is necessary that \( \sigma' \) and \( \sigma \) differ by a single adjacent transposition. Thus, the problem reduces to constructing a sequence \( \sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_{m/2} \) where \( \sigma_i \) and \( \sigma_{i+1} \) differ by an adjacent transposition (\( 1 \leq i \leq m/2 \)), and the set \( \{\sigma_i\}_{1 \leq i \leq m/2} \) together with their reverses covers every permutation exactly once.  

For \( n = 4 \), a construction exists. For \( n \geq 5 \), we proceed by induction on \( n \): each time, move \( n \) from the front of the permutation to the back (or vice versa), then perform the construction for \( n-1 \) as per the inductive hypothesis. Note that \( (n-1)!/2 \) is even, which completes the induction.  

For \( n = 4 \), the construction is as follows:  
\[ (1, 2, 3, 4), (2, 1, 3, 4), (2, 1, 4, 3), (1, 2, 4, 3), (1, 4, 2, 3), (4, 1, 2, 3), (4, 1, 3, 2), (1, 4, 3, 2), (1, 3, 4, 2), (3, 1, 4, 2), (3, 1, 2, 4), (1, 3, 2, 4). \]

stem_md:
Given positive integers \( n, k \), let \( S = \{1, 2, \cdots, n\} \). For each subset \( I \) of \( S \), assign a non-negative real number \( X_I \), and define  $Y_I = \sum_{J \subseteq I} X_J.$  

It is given that \( Y_S = 1 \), and for any subsets \( I, J \subseteq S \), whenever \( I \subseteq J \),  $X_I \leq X_J.$  Determine the minimum possible value of  
\[\sum_{I \subseteq S} (-1)^{n-|I|} Y_I^{k},\]  
where \( |I| \) denotes the number of elements in the finite set \( I \). 

*Created by Cheng Jiang*
solution_md:
Since
\begin{align*}\sum_{I \subseteq S} (-1)^{n-|I|} Y_I^{k}&=\sum_{I \subseteq S} (-1)^{n-|I|} \sum_{J_1,\cdots ,J_k\subseteq I}X_{J_1}X_{J_2}\cdots X_{J_k}&=\sum_{J_1,\cdots ,J_k\subseteq S}X_{J_1}X_{J_2}\cdots X_{J_k}\sum_{J_1,\cdots ,J_k\subseteq I} (-1)^{n-|I|}&=\sum_{J_1\sqcup \cdots\sqcup J_k=S}X_{J_1}X_{J_2}\cdots X_{J_k}.\end{align*}
Note that it is easy to verify that if  $S_1\subseteq S_2$ , then
\[\sum_{J_1\sqcup \cdots\sqcup J_k=S_2}X_{J_1}X_{J_2}\cdots X_{J_k}\ge \sum_{J_1\sqcup \cdots\sqcup J_k=S_1}X_{J_1}X_{J_2}\cdots X_{J_k}.\]
Thus we get the desired minimum value  ${\left(1-\frac 1{2^k}\right)^n}.\Box$

stem_md:
Given positive integers \(a_1, a_2, \cdots, a_{100}, b_1, b_2, \cdots, b_{100}\) satisfying \(a_1 < a_2 < \cdots < a_{100}, \) \(b_1 < b_2 < \cdots < b_{100}\), and the  $100$  integers   $a_1 - b_1, \, a_2 - b_2, \, \cdots, \, a_{100} - b_{100}$  are parawise distinct. 

Find the minimum possible value of \(\max\{a_{100}, b_{100}\}\). 

*Proposed by Tianqin Li*
solution_md:
Replace  $100$  with  $n$ . The answer is  $\boxed{2n-1}$ , attained when  $a_i:=2i-1$  and  $b_i:=i$ .

Note that subtracting any constant from either sequence preserves the property.

We use induction on  $n$  with the base case trivial.

Suppose all the  $a_i-b_i$  are either all nonpositive or nonnegative, WLOG nonnegative. Suppose FTSOC  $a_n,\,b_n\leq 2n-2$ . Note that  $i\leq a_i,\,b_i\leq n-2+i$ . Thus  $a_i-b_i\leq n-2$  so there are only  $n-1$  possible values of  $a_i-b_i$  over all  $i\in[n]$ , a contradiction.

Now assume  $a_i-b_i$  achieves both positive and negative values over all  $i\in [n]$ . Notice that one of  $a_1-b_1$  or  $a_n-b_n$  will be nonzero. WLOG assume  $a_1-b_1$  is nonzero and positive. Let  $m\geq 1$  be minimal such that  $a_{m+1}\leq b_{m+1}$ . Then  $a_m>b_m$ . Apply the induction hypothesis to the sequences  $a_1-1,\,\ldots,\,a_m-1$  and  $b_1,\,\ldots,\,b_m$  to get  $a_m-1\geq 2m-1$ . Thus  $a_{m+1}\geq 2m+1$ . Apply the induction hypothesis to the sequences  $a_{m+1}-2m,\,\ldots,\,a_n-2m$  and  $b_{m+1}-2m,\,\ldots,\,b_n-2m$  to get  $\max\{a_n-2m,\,b_n-2m\}\geq 2(n-m)-1$ . Thus  $\max\{a_n,\,b_n\}\geq 2n-1$ , completing the induction step.  $\square$
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/China Contests/Shu Zhi Mi Mathematical Olympiad/2025 August SZM Mathematical Olympiad/3644831.json

candidates:
For the construction: $a_i = 2i-1$  $b_i = i$ which obviously works. 
Now suppose for some  $i: 2i-1>a_i>b_i \ge 1.$  By the condition of the problem there can be at most one equal among  $a_i$  and  $b_i$ , then there are  $i$  numbers from  $a_1$  to  $a_i$  and similarly  $i$  distinct numbers from  $b_1$  to  $b_i$ , then there is at least  $2i-1$  distinct numbers among them which is a contradiction. $a_{100} \ge 200-1=199$

The answer is  $199$ . Take  $a_i = 2i - 1$  and  $b_i = i$  we have  $c_i := a_i - b_i = i-1$ .

For the bound, let  $c_k$  be the maximum among all those  $c_i$ 's and  $c_l$  be the minimum, we then have  $c_k - c_l \ge 99$ . We may assume that  $k>l$  as we can swap  $a_i$  with  $a_{101-i}$  and  $b_i$  with  $b_{101-i}$ .

Now consider  $a_k$ ,  $a_l$ ,  $b_k$ ,  $b_l$ . The optimal case should be  $l=1$ ,  $a_l=b_l=1$  and  $k=100$  is such that  $a_k$  is maximised. So we try to bound subjecting to these constraints. We want to show  $a_{100} \ge 199$  because this will mean  $\max\{a_{100},b_{100}\} \ge a_{100} \ge 199$ . The way to bring  $a_{100}$  into the game is  $a_{100} - a_k \ge 100 - k$ .

Firstly,  $a_k - b_k - (a_l - b_l) \ge 99 \implies a_k \ge 99 + b_k - b_l + a_l$ . We have  $b_k - b_l \ge k-l$ , and it's subjecting to the equality condition so far so we are good.

To eliminate  $a_l$ , we use  $a_l \ge l$ . From the previous inequality  $a_k \le a_{100} + k - 100$ .

In conclusion,   $$ a_{100} + k - 100 \ge a_k \ge 99 + b_k - b_l + a_l \ge 99 + k - l + a_l \ge 99 + k, $$  so  $a_{100} \ge 199$  as desired.

stem_md:
Let complex sequence \(\{z_n\}\) satisfy: \(z_1 = 0, \, z_2 = i\), and for any integer \(n \geq 3\),  
\[z_n = 3i \cdot \overline{z_{n-1}} - 2z_{n-2}.\]  
Denote \(z = z_1 + z_2 + \cdots + z_{2025}\). Find the imaginary part of \(z\). 

*Proposed by Tianqin Li*
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>I claimed that  $z_n=(2^{n-1}-1)i$  when  $n=2,4,\dots$  and  $z_n=2^{n-1}-1$ ; otherwise. 
We will prove this using mathematical induction over  $n\in\mathbb{N}$  where the base cases  $n=1,2$  are obvious.
Given a positive integer  $k\in\mathbb{N}$ . We may split into two cases:

    
- Suppose that  $k$  is an odd integer. Assume further  $z_k=2^{k-1}-1$  and  $z_{k-1}=(2^{k-2}-1)i$ .
    Consider the expression
    \begin{align*}
        z_{k+1}&=3i\cdot \overline{z_{k}}-2z_{k-1}&=3i(2^{k-1}-1)-2i(2^{k-2}-1)
        &=i(3\cdot 2^{k-1}-2^{k-1}-1)
        &=i(2^k-1).
    \end{align*}
- Suppose that  $k$  is an even integer. Assume further  $z_k=(2^{k-1}-1)i$  and  $z_{k-1}=2^{k-2}-1$ .
    Consider the expression
    \begin{align*}
        z_{k+1}&=3i\cdot \overline{z_{k}}-2z_{k-1}
        &=-3i(2^{k-1}-1)i-2(2^{k-2}-1)
        &=3(2^{k-1}-1)-2(2^{k-2}-1)
        &=2^k-1.
    \end{align*}

Lastly, we may evaluate the imaginary part of  $z$  as  $$ \mathrm{Im}(z)=\sum_{k=1}^{1012}(2^{2k-1}-1)=2\cdot\frac{4^{1012}-1}{3}-1012. $$</details>

Let \( \mathbb{Z}^2 \) denote the set of all integer lattice points in the plane with Cartesian coordinates. A graph \( G = (\mathbb{Z}^2, E) \) is constructed by connecting two lattice points with an edge if their Euclidean distance is  $1{}{}{}$ . For a positive integer \( n \), define \( f(n) \) as the number of connected subgraphs \( H = (V(H), E(H)) \) of \( G \) satisfying:  
\[
\{(0, 0)\} \subseteq V(H) \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^2, \quad |V(H)| = n, \quad E(H) \subseteq E.
\]  
Prove that there exists a positive constant \( C \) such that for any positive integer \( n \),  \(
f(n) \leq C \cdot 7^n.
\)

*Proposed by Hanqing Huang and Huankun Guo*

candidates:
900th post! No idea what to post so just give the proposer's nice idea:
------
Let \( p \in (0, 1) \) be a specific real number. Consider selecting each edge with probability \( p \), resulting in a random subgraph of \( \mathbb{Z}^2 \). The probability that the connected component containing the origin has exactly \( n \) vertices is  
\[
\sum_{\substack{G \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^2  |V(G)| = n  G \text{ connected}}} p^{|E(G)|} (1 - p)^{|\partial E(G)|},
\]  
where \( \partial E(G) \) denotes the set of edges with exactly one endpoint in \( V(G) \).  

Observe that  
\[
4 |V(G)| = \sum_{v \in V(G)} 4 = \sum_{v \in V(G)} \sum_{\substack{u \in \mathbb{Z}^2  u \sim v}} 1 \geq \sum_{e \in E(G)} 2 + \sum_{e \in \partial E(G)} 1 = 2 |E(G)| + |\partial E(G)|.
\]  
By setting \( p = \frac{3 - \sqrt{5}}{2} \) (noting that \( p = (1 - p)^2 \)), and since the computed probability is at most 1, we obtain  
\[
1 \geq \sum_{\substack{G \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^2  |V(G)| = n  G \text{ connected}}} \left( \frac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{2} \right)^{2|E(G)| + |\partial E(G)|} \geq f(n) \left( \frac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{2} \right)^{4n}.
\]  
Thus,  
\[
f(n) \leq \left( \frac{\sqrt{5} + 1}{2} \right)^{4n} \leq 7^n.\Box
\]

stem_md: Find the largest real number  $C$ , such that for all  $98$  positive real numbers  $x_1,x_2, \cdots, x_{98}$ , if  $ \sum_{i=1}^{98}{x_i}=98$ , there always exists a permutation of  $(x_i)$ , call it  $(y_i)$ , satisfies: $\sum_{i=1}^{98}{[y_i+ \frac{i}{10}]}>C$
solution_md:
Answer is 529. For any real number \( x \), by Hermite's identity, we have:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{98} \left\lfloor x + \frac{i}{10} \right\rfloor = 10 \lfloor 10x \rfloor + 450 - \lfloor x \rfloor - \lfloor x + 9.9 \rfloor
\]
\[
> 10 (10x - 1) + 450 - x - (x + 9.9) = 98x + 430.1.
\]
Thus,
\[
\frac{1}{98} \sum_{k=1}^{98} \sum_{i=1}^{98} \left\lfloor x_k + \frac{i}{10} \right\rfloor > \sum_{k=1}^{98} x_k + 430.1 = 528.1.
\]
By PHP there exists a permutation \( y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_{98} \) of \( x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{98} \) such that
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{98} \left\lfloor y_i + \frac{i}{10} \right\rfloor > 528.1.\Box
\]
Equality holds when  $x_1=\cdots=x_{97}=0.2-\epsilon$  and  $x_{98}=78.6+97\epsilon$  (easy to verify)

solution_md:
Cute :maybe:

If  $a$  is odd, use  $a\to a(1-\frac 1a)=a-1$ , we don't do operation if  $a$  is even.

stem_md:
Let  $P$  be a convex polygon with centroid  $G$ , and let  $\mathcal P$  be the set of vertices of  $P$ . Let  $\mathcal X$  be the set of triangles with vertices all in  $\mathcal P$ . We sort the elements  $\triangle ABC$  of  $\mathcal X$  into the following three categories:


- (Type 1)  $G$  lies in the strict interior of  $\triangle ABC$ ; let  $\mathcal A$  be the set of triangles of this type.
- (Type 2)  $G$  lies in the strict exterior of  $\triangle ABC$ ; let  $\mathcal B$  be the set of triangles of this type.
- (Type 3)  $G$  lies on the boundary of  $\triangle ABC$ .

For any triangle  $T$ , denote by  $S_T$  the area of  $T$ . Prove that \[\sum_{T \in \mathcal A} S_T \geq \sum_{T \in \mathcal B} S_T.\]
solution_md:
This is an incredibly difficult and elegant problem. I'll share partial official soltion.
------
Connect the centroid to each vertex to form vectors, labeled clockwise as \(v_1, v_2, \cdots, v_n\). after **many efforts** it suffices to prove  
\[
\left( \sum_{1 \leq i < j \leq n} v_i \times v_j \right) \geq 0.
\]  
For \(1 \leq j \leq n\), let \(v_j = r_j e^{i\theta_j}\), where \(r_j \in \mathbb{R}\) and \(\theta_j \in [0, \pi)\). Let \(x_j = r_j \sin \theta_j\). Then,  
\[
\sum_{j=1}^n r_j e^{i\theta_j} = \sum_{j=1}^n v_i = 0 \Rightarrow \sum_{j=1}^n x_j = 0.
\]  
For \(1 \leq i \leq n\), define \(\chi_{x \leq a_i}\) as the indicator function, which takes the value 1 when \(x \leq a_i\) and 0 otherwise. We then have  
\[
\sum_{1 \leq i < j \leq n} v_i \times v_j = - \sum_{1 \leq i < j \leq n} r_i r_j |\sin(\theta_i - \theta_j)| = - \sum_{1 \leq i < j \leq n} x_i x_j |\cot \theta_i - \cot \theta_j|.
\]  
Let \(a_j = \cot \theta_j\). Then:  
\begin{align*}
\sum_{1 \leq i < j \leq n} v_i \times v_j &= - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{1 \leq i,j \leq n} x_i x_j |a_i - a_j| 
&= - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{1 \leq i,j \leq n} x_i x_j (a_i + a_j - 2 \min\{a_i, a_j\}) 
&= - \left( \sum_{i=1}^n x_i \right) \left( \sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i \right) + \sum_{1 \leq i,j \leq n} x_i x_j \int_0^\infty \chi_{x \leq a_i}(x) \chi_{x \leq a_j}(x) \, dx 
&= \int_0^\infty \left( \sum_{i=1}^n x_i \chi_{x \leq a_i}(x) \right)^2 dx \geq 0,
\end{align*}  
which completes the proof.   $\Box$

solution_md: This is the partial case of the setup from Barany's and Grinbergs theorem [1]. In the real $d$ -dimensional [tip=normed space]the norm is not necessarily Euclidean[/tip] they consider $n$ [tip=balanced sets]i.e. $0$ lies in $\operatorname{conv}V_i$ [/tip] sets $V_1, \ldots, V_n$ in the unit ball. Define a transversal of $V_1, \ldots, V_n$ as any set $T=\{v_1, \ldots, v_n\}$ where $v_i\in V_i$ . They show that there exists a universal constant $C(d)$ depending on $d$ (but not on $n$ ) such that there exists a transversal $T$ of $V_1, \ldots, V_n$ with short sum, i.e. $\|\sum_{v\in T}v\|\le C(d)$ . They prove this for $C(d)\le d$ . For the Euclidean norm I improve this bound to $C(d)\le \sqrt d$ (one of the results in my bachelor's thesis [2]). The bound is sharp, it is reached for $n=d$ and $V_i = \{e_i, -e_i\}$ where $e_1, \ldots, e_d$ is the orthonormal basis in $\mathbb R^d$ . Actually this result was proved almost at the same time independently (but essentially using the same method) by Ambrus and Bozzai [3]. This problem (#1) adds the constraint that $\sum_{v\in V_i}v=0$ for all $i\in[n]$ (in addition to balancedness). It is a bit unnatural and surprising for such a setup to appear on a high school contest. Anyway the answer to this problem is obviously the answer of the more general problem described above, $\min C = \sqrt d$ (since the construction $V_i=\{\pm e_i\}$ applies here too). [1] I. Bárány, V.S. Grinberg, *[On some combinatorial questions in finite-dimensional spaces](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0024379581900859)* [2] S. Harutyunyan (supervised by A. Polyanskii), [*Variations of the theorem of Barany and Grinberg about vector sums*](https://github.com/saro2808/website/blob/main/static/documents/%D0%94%D0%B8%D0%BF%D0%BB%D0%BE%D0%BC-4.pdf) (in Russian) [3] G. Ambrus, R. Bozzai, *[Colorful Vector Balancing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.10865)*

We actually developed the problem on our own. We only use the fact that  $0$  is in the convex hull. In fact, this can be easily seen equivalent with zero sums since we can duplicate elements in  $A_i$  arbitrary number of times. 
Consider independent probability distributions  $B_i$  on  $A_i$  such that  $\mathbb{E}(\sum_i B_i)=0$ . A possible construction is the uniform distribution for each  $i$ . Clearly  $\text{Var}(B_i)=\mathbb E{|B_i|}^2-|\mathbb E(b_i)|^2\le 1$  for each  $i$ .
Claim: There are possible  $B_i$ s with at most  $d$  being non-constant.
Proof: Let  $c_i$  be the number of possible(with nonzero probability) results of  $B_i$ . Find the alignment with the minimum  $S=\sum_i(c_i-1)$ . If  $S>d$ , we can reassign the probabilities to make  $S$  smaller by dimension counting.  
Now we have  $\mathbb E(|\sum_i B_i|^2)=|\mathbb E(\sum_i B_i)|^2+\sum_i \text{Var}(B_i)\le d$  as desired.
This solution also generalizes to general norms.

Same as @above

Let  $|z_1^2+z_1z_2+z_2^2| = \frac{1}{4}|(z_1+2z_2)^2+3z_1^2| \le 1$  so  $3|z_1|^2 \le 5$  and  $|z_1| \le \frac{\sqrt5}{\sqrt3}$ . stem_md:
Let \( m \geq 3 \) be an integer, and let \( \mathcal F \) denote the set of all permutations of \(\{1, 2, \cdots, m\}\).  

Let \( n \) be a positive integer. Consider an \( n \times n \) grid, where initially each cell of the grid is filled with a permutation from \( \mathcal F \). An operation is defined as follows: select a permutation \( \tau \in \mathcal F \) and choose a row or column of the grid, then for each cell in the selected row (or column), replace the current permutation \( \sigma \) in the cell with \( \sigma \circ \tau \). Let \( f(n) \) be the smallest integer such that for any initial configuration of permutations in the grid, if it is possible to transform all permutations into the identity permutation through a finite number of operations, then this can be achieved in no more than \( f(n) \) operations.  

Prove that there exist positive real numbers \( c_1 < c_2 \) such that for any integer \( n \geq 3 \), the following holds:  
\[c_1 \cdot \frac{n^2}{\ln n} < f(n) < c_2 \cdot \frac{n^2}{\ln n} \]
solution_md:
Hinted? accidentally I think. ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Note that the sign of a permutation is a map from $\mathcal{F}$ to $\{ \pm 1\}$ which maps composition to multiplication. For this to be possible, we must have that if we consider the grid of signs $\mathbb{F}_2^{n^2}$ , we can toggle rows or columns to get all the signs to be $1$ . Since this is commutative, there are essentially $4^n$ configurations of signs. Now, note that $(23)((12)(34))(23)((12)(34)) = (14)(23)$ is a commutator in $\mathcal{F}$ , so since any even permutation may be expressed as the product of an even number of transpositions, by applying this commutator to the rows and columns we can solve any even configuration. ------------------- **Bounding** Note that there are $m! \cdot 2n$ possible moves available at each turn. Since there are $4^n (m!/2)^{n^2}$ possible configurations, it follows that \[ (m! \cdot 2n)^{f(n)} > 4^n (m!/2)^{n^2} \implies f(n) > \frac{n^2 \cdot \ln(m!/2)}{\ln(m! \cdot 2n)} + O(n) \] so $c_1 = \ln(m!/2) - \varepsilon$ works for any $\varepsilon$ for sufficently large $n$ . ------------------- **Construction** We may first spend $O(n)$ turns to make all the permutation entries have even sign. We can spend $4$ moves to apply a disjoint product of two transpositions, and each permutation can be written as at most $m$ pairs of disjoint transpositions. The first key insight is that we want to able to apply a commutator to all applicable areas at once. As such, we spend at most $4 \cdot m \cdot 3 \cdot \binom{m}{4} \cdot N$ moves, where $N$ is from the following, as we iterate $\frac{m}{2}$ over all
Take an $n \times n$ table over $\mathbb{F}_2$ . We may, for a cost of $i+j$ , toggle the elements in the intersection of $i$ rows and $j$ columns. Then we need cost at most $N$ to turn any table into the identity.
The idea now is that we can solve an $n \times \ln(n)$ grid with cost at most $n + \ln(n) \cdot 2^{\ln(n)} = n + o(1)$ as follows. Each row is one of $2^{\ln(n)}$ possible tuples, and if there are $c_i$ occurences of the $i$ th tuple, we may spend cost $c_i + \ln(n)$ to toggle all applicable rows. Since the sum of $c_i$ is $n$ , the bound follows. This means that $N$ is equal to $\frac{n^2}{\ln(n)} + O(1)$ , so $c_2 = \frac{m^5}{2}$ works as an upper bound. -------------------------------------------------------------**Remark:** I think both the bound and construction are pretty hard to find. It didn't take me long at all to find the subproblem, but it took me a decent while to find the bound, and I somewhat got hinted on the construction; In retrospect, I was too focused on trying to get $i$ to be equal-ish to $j$ , when it suffices really to have the sum of $i$ be large-ish. I was also stuck on trying to get the rows to be a completely all $1$ s. Nonetheless, a key idea between algorithmic / asymptotic problems like this is choosing your variables to have the right size, and this is a very cool example of this.
